title: Check a suspicious approach through official channels
summary: General Singapore guidance for checking suspicious messages, numbers and links before acting.
evidence: When a message may be a scam, check it through ScamShield or call the 24/7 ScamShield Helpline at 1799 before acting.
actions: Pause before replying, clicking or paying.
Use ScamShield or call 1799 if the approach remains uncertain.

title: Immediate response after money was transferred
summary: Official steps to limit further financial loss after a scam transfer.
evidence: If money or card access may be compromised, contact the bank immediately, then file a police report and preserve relevant transaction details.
actions: Contact the bank immediately to halt further transactions.
File a police report online or at a police post.

title: Secure compromised accounts and warn contacts
summary: Official account-security steps after credentials or online accounts may have been exposed.
evidence: If an email or social account may be compromised, change its password, enable two-factor authentication, inform contacts and report the incident to the service provider.
actions: Change affected passwords from a trusted device.
Enable two-factor authentication and notify contacts.

title: Government officers do not request safe-account transfers
summary: Impersonators allege criminal involvement and demand transfers or valuables for an investigation.
evidence: Singapore government officials will not ask over a phone call for money to be moved to a safe account or for cash, gold or valuables to be handed over for investigation.
actions: Do not transfer funds or hand over valuables.
Contact the named agency through independently obtained details.

title: Government officers do not request credentials or unofficial apps
summary: Official guidance on credential, app-installation and call-transfer red flags.
evidence: Government officials will not ask for bank log-in, Singpass or CPF information, require apps from unofficial stores, or transfer a call to the Police.
actions: Do not reveal credentials or OTPs.
Do not install software supplied by an unsolicited caller.

title: Verify Singapore government SMS identity independently
summary: Guidance for checking messages that claim to be from Singapore government agencies.
evidence: Government SMS messages normally use the gov.sg Sender ID; personal information quoted by a caller is not proof that the caller is genuine.
actions: Check the sender and contact the agency directly.
Call 1799 if the identity remains uncertain.

title: Fake MOM rectification documents can install malware
summary: A malware scam uses fake MOM emails, websites and compressed rectification documents.
evidence: SPF warns that unsolicited emails impersonating MOM may link to fake pages and compressed rectification files that install malware and enable remote access.
actions: Do not open unfamiliar compressed files.
Verify an alleged MOM notice through official MOM channels.

title: High-return, low-risk promises and time pressure
summary: Common investment-scam promises and pressure tactics.
evidence: Promises of unusually high returns with low or no risk, combined with limited-time pressure, are common warning signs of a phony investment.
actions: Do not invest under time pressure.
Discuss the offer with someone trusted and verify it independently.

title: Fake profits and withdrawal-fee escalation
summary: Fake platforms show early profits before blocking withdrawal and demanding more money.
evidence: Scammers may display apparent profits or pay a small early return, then block withdrawals and demand tax, verification or release fees before funds can be obtained.
actions: Do not transfer more money to unlock a withdrawal.
Contact the bank immediately if funds were already sent.

title: Check a claimed investment firm in the MAS directory
summary: The official MAS directory identifies regulated financial institutions and their licences.
evidence: Verify a financial firm and its permitted activities in the official MAS Financial Institutions Directory rather than using a link supplied by the promoter.
actions: Search the firm in the MAS directory.
Contact it using details obtained from an official source.

title: Unsolicited online investment contacts and chat groups
summary: Investment scams often begin with online strangers, recommendations or unknown chat groups.
evidence: Treat investment recommendations from online strangers or unknown chat groups cautiously, especially when testimonials and success stories are used to prompt transfers.
actions: Leave and report suspicious investment groups.
Verify the entity through MAS and an official company hotline.

title: Simple-task jobs should not require advance payment
summary: Task and commission scams ask job seekers to fund purchases, ratings or online tasks.
evidence: An online job is likely fraudulent if it promises commission for simple tasks but requires an upfront transfer or use of personal funds to continue.
actions: Do not pay a deposit or fund tasks.
Verify the vacancy with the company directly.

title: Do not use a personal bank account for a job
summary: Some fake jobs recruit people to transfer funds through their own accounts for commission.
evidence: A job that requires receiving or forwarding money through a personal bank account can expose the participant to scam-mule activity and financial loss.
actions: Do not receive or forward money for a recruiter.
Contact the bank if the account has already been used.

title: Recruiters should not request Singpass credentials
summary: Job scams may request Singpass passwords or a QR-code scan as supposed recruitment verification.
evidence: A recruiter asking for a Singpass password, passcode or QR-code scan to apply for a job is a strong scam indicator.
actions: Do not share Singpass credentials or scan an unsolicited QR code.
Verify the recruiter with the employer independently.

title: Keep marketplace payments on the platform
summary: Direct payment outside a marketplace removes platform protections and is a common scam sign.
evidence: A seller asking for PayNow or another direct payment instead of the platform's secure payment option is a strong warning sign.
actions: Use the marketplace's secure checkout only.
Report a seller who insists on off-platform payment.

title: Sellers should verify payment before releasing goods
summary: Fake buyers may send fabricated screenshots as supposed proof of payment.
evidence: Marketplace sellers should confirm that funds actually arrived in their own account rather than relying on a screenshot or message supplied by a buyer.
actions: Check the banking or marketplace app directly.
Do not release an item based only on a payment screenshot.

title: Unexpected delivery fees, links and third-party apps
summary: Extra customs or delivery fees and seller-supplied links or apps are common e-commerce scam patterns.
evidence: Be cautious when a seller or delivery message demands an additional customs fee, directs payment through a link, or asks for installation of a third-party app.
actions: Check the order inside the marketplace or courier's official app.
Do not use seller-supplied payment links or apps.

title: Unsolicited links that request passwords, card details or OTPs
summary: Phishing messages impersonate trusted organisations and use spoofed pages to steal credentials.
evidence: Do not use unsolicited links or QR codes to enter passwords, banking credentials, card details or OTPs; verify the real address independently.
actions: Open the organisation's known app or type its address yourself.
Contact the account provider if details were entered.

title: Banks do not send clickable login links by SMS
summary: Bank phishing SMS messages use urgent account alerts and embedded login links.
evidence: Banks will not send clickable links by SMS for account login; check an alert through the official banking app and registered sender information.
actions: Do not open the SMS link.
Check the transaction in the official banking app or call the bank.

title: Parcel-delivery messages can lead to phishing pages
summary: Messages impersonating postal and logistics companies may contain credential or card-stealing links.
evidence: Verify an unexpected parcel or redelivery notice directly with the courier or e-commerce platform instead of using the message's link.
actions: Check tracking in the courier's official app or site.
Do not enter card or banking details through the message link.

title: IRAS refund messages should be checked in myTax Portal
summary: Tax-refund phishing may request card details or confidential information through email links.
evidence: IRAS tax refunds are not processed to credit or debit cards; check refund status through myTax Portal and do not pay a third-party account.
actions: Open myTax Portal independently to check the refund.
Do not disclose banking credentials, card details or OTPs.

source: Singapore Police Force and Cyber Security Agency of Singapore
title: Microsoft-style pop-ups with support numbers are a scam sign
summary: Technical-support scams use alarming browser alerts and phone numbers to initiate contact.
evidence: Microsoft does not include phone numbers in error or warning messages; do not call, click or interact with an unsolicited security pop-up.
actions: Close the browser or use Task Manager if necessary.
Verify any alert through the software provider's official support channel.

source: Singapore Police Force and Cyber Security Agency of Singapore
title: Respond after granting remote device access
summary: Remote-access scams use AnyDesk, UltraViewer or similar tools to take over devices and banking sessions.
evidence: If remote access was granted, disconnect or power off the device, contact the bank, remove the software, run an anti-virus scan, change credentials on a trusted device and report the incident.
actions: Disconnect the affected device and call the bank immediately.
Remove remote-access software and change credentials from another trusted device.

title: Keep Singpass passwords, passcodes and OTPs confidential
summary: Official Singpass security guidance and support for suspected account compromise.
evidence: Singpass personnel will not ask for a password, passcode or SMS OTP; suspected compromise should be reported through the official Singpass Helpdesk.
actions: Do not reveal a Singpass password, passcode or OTP.
Use the official Singpass Helpdesk if the account may be compromised.
